name: Barbell + plates

lead: A barbell is a long steel bar with rotating sleeves onto which weight plates are loaded, typically paired with a rack and bench. The standard Olympic bar weighs 20 kg for men and 15 kg for women and accepts small plate increments.

It is the backbone of strength and physique training because squats, deadlifts, presses and rows can all be loaded heavily and in small steps. Proponents say this allows the largest muscles (legs, back, chest, shoulders) to be built systematically, which they describe as affecting overall proportions more than isolation gadgets.

paras: Progressive overload is the underlying principle: adding weight over time forces muscle and connective tissue to adapt. Meta-analyses show hypertrophy is similar across a broad range of loads taken near failure, while heavier loading maximizes strength, so a barbell can serve both aims. Fine plate jumps make it practical to keep progressing for years.

The barbell has a high ceiling for both benefit and injury. Poor technique, lifting beyond one's ability, missing safeties and training alone under heavy loads are the usual causes of harm. Cost and space are considerations: a bar, plates, rack, bench and flooring add up. The evidence for resistance training with heavy free weights is strong; product claims are mostly about durability and specification rather than efficacy.
